chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from Ali ibn al-Salt from Bakr ibn Muhammad from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

A questioner asked him about the time of Maghrib prayer. He said: 'Indeed Allah, the Exalted, says in His Book to Ibrahim (peace be upon him): "When the night covered him, he saw a star." This is the beginning of the time, and its end is the disappearance of the red glow (shafaq). And the beginning of the time of 'Isha is the disappearance of the redness, and its end is until the darkness of the night, meaning the middle of the night.'

And what Sad ibn Abdillah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Abu Hammam Ismail ibn Hammam said: I saw al-Rida (peace be upon him) and we were with him; he did not pray Maghrib until the stars appeared. Then he stood up and prayed with us at the door of the house of Ibn Abi Mahmud.

key_terms.اَلشَّفَق: Shafaq (the red twilight glow after sunset)
key_terms.غَسَقُ اَللَّيْلِ: Ghasaq al-layl (the darkness of the night, specifically the middle)

ai.seo_question: What are the precise astronomical signs that mark the beginning and end of Maghrib and 'Isha prayer times in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) elucidates the precise astronomical markers for prayer times, linking the start of Maghrib to the appearance of the first star as referenced in the Quranic narrative of Ibrahim. This narration highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on distinguishing between the disappearance of the red twilight (shafaq) for Maghrib's end and the onset of full darkness for 'Isha, a distinction crucial for determining the validity of delayed prayers. The supporting report of Imam al-Rida (peace be upon him) demonstrates the practical application of these definitions, showing flexibility in delaying Maghrib until star visibility, which aligns with the opinion of many jurists.
